questions.q: A study reports a 95% confidence interval $[42.9, 56.1]$ for a mean $\mu$. Which statement is correct?
options: There is a 95% probability that $\mu$ lies in $[42.9, 56.1]$
95% of the data points lie in $[42.9, 56.1]$
If the study were repeated many times, about 95% of the intervals built this way would contain $\mu$
The sample mean has a 95% chance of being in the interval
questions.explain: $\mu$ is fixed, so this particular interval either contains it or not. The 95% is a property of the *procedure* — exactly what the 100-interval coverage plot shows. The interval is about the mean, not individual data points.

options: The probability that $H_0$ is true given the data
The probability, assuming $H_0$ is true, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed
The probability of making a Type II error
The size of the effect divided by its standard error
questions.explain: It is the tail area of the null distribution beyond the observed statistic (the shaded region in the A/B lab). It is *not* $P(H_0\mid\text{data})$; the last option describes the $z$ statistic itself.

questions.q: An A/B test has 80% power to detect a 1-percentage-point lift. Roughly how many users per arm do you need for the same power if the true lift is only 0.5 points?
questions.explain: The required sample size scales like $1/\Delta^2$: halving the effect size quadruples $n$, because the standard error only shrinks like $1/\sqrt n$.

questions.q: You run 20 independent tests at $\alpha = 0.05$ where no real effect exists. What is the probability of at least one 'significant' result, and what Bonferroni threshold would you use?
questions.explain: $1 - 0.95^{20} \approx 0.64$. Bonferroni tests each hypothesis at $\alpha/m = 0.0025$, which keeps the family-wise error rate at or below 5%.
